titleStmt.title: True Digital Poiesis: A Conceptual Framework and Interface Design for Generative AI in the Humanities

dhq:bio.p: Dr. Will Hasty is Professor of German Studies and Co-Director of the Center for Medieval and Early Modern Studies. He has published widely on medieval and early modern literary culture, particularly on medieval romance narratives. He is author of numerous books and articles and has edited many collections of essays and literary encyclopedias. Besides his more strictly literary interests, he has maintained ongoing interests in Generative AI, Computational Philology, Narrative Theory, Neomedievalism, Virtual Reality, and Digital Cultural Studies. He has been founding director of the Sustainable Online Network for Global-Cultural Studies (SONGS) Initiative (2017-present); Waldo W. Neikirk Professor of German and Medieval and Early Modern Studies (2017-2022); Member of the Imagining the Technosphere Mellon Intersections Group (2018-2021); and LLC Coordinator of German Studies (2008-present). He twice served as Chair of the Department of Germanic and Slavic Studies (2004-2005 and 2008-2009). He is cocreator of the German Grammar Cruncher Language Learning Application collaboratively developed by German Studies and the University of Florida Center for Instructional Technology. Since 2024 he has been Co-PI on a $17,159 grant from the University of Florida Artificial Intelligence and Informatics Research Institute, applying literary, poetic, and historical analysis to identify the limitations of generative AI and develop solutions that improve human-AI interaction in the humanities.

Dr. Mark Law is a Distinguished Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering. Dr. Law was named an IEEE Fellow in 1998 for his contributions to integrated circuit process modeling and simulation. He has won several national and international awards based on this work including a 1992 NSF Presidential Faculty Fellow, 1993 SRC Technical Excellence Award, the 2006 SRC Aristotle Award for Outstanding Graduate Student Advising, the 2010 IEEE EDS J.J. Ebers Award, the 2013 SIA University Research Award, and the 2013 SEMI North America award. At UF, he has been named the College of Engineering Teacher of the Year in 1996-97 and a UF Research Fellow in 1998. In 2019, he was named to the UF Academy of Distinguished Teaching Scholars. In 2020, he was named the Outstanding Undergraduate Mentor in the College of Engineering. Dr. Law has written over 200 papers on process and device modeling and has advised more than 25 Ph.D. students. He has been involved in more than $25 million of funding during his career. In addition to IEEE, he is a member of the Electrochemical Society, American Physical Society, and American Society for Engineering Education. His current teaching interests are in the intersection of humanities, social science, and engineering. He is also active in the arts and has been an associate producer of the off Broadway hit Puffs: Or Seven Increasingly Eventful Years at a Certain School of Magic and Magic and, on Broadway, Slava's Snowshow. He is also a backer of the recent revival of Sweeney Todd, The Demon Barber of Fleet Street. He is a founding investor of the Twenty-Sided Tavern, an interactive theater experience.

Dr. Daniel Maxwell brings a background in History and French to a career built primarily around technology, carrying forward the values of a classical liberal arts education into his technical work. He seeks to position his work at the intersection of technology and the humanities and serves as the designated liaison to humanities faculty for the Research Computing department at the University of Florida, providing support and advice on how to apply machine learning technologies to advance our understanding of truth. Dr. Maxwell has a special interest in Medieval / Renaissance culture as well as the art and literature of that period.

Lauren Dulick graduated May 2026 as a Computer Science and Engineering student and University Research Scholar at the University of Florida. Her coursework and research center on software engineering, data structures, and applied machine learning. As a researcher with the University Research Scholars Program, she has explored applications of AI in interdisciplinary contexts, including a deep learning project relating depression diagnoses to homelife variables and a study of ethical decision-making frameworks for autonomous vehicles. She has also developed full-stack software applications for the University of Florida's Center for Outdoor Recreation and Education and served as a Software Engineering Intern at GlobalWafers America, where she automated manufacturing tool operations in C#. She is a member of the Society of Women Engineers and the Real-World Engineering Club.

Dr. S. Ying Xiao is an associate professor of global Chinese studies and film and media studies at the University of Florida. Her teaching and research interests primarily concentrate on transnational Chinese/Sinophone films, Chinese and Asians in the global context, Classical Hollywood cinema in the sound era, popular music, youth culture, sound studies, theories of globalization and transnationalism, Buddhism and film, and the discourse of gender and sexuality. She is the book author of China in the Mix: Cinema, Sound, and Popular Culture in the Age of Globalization (University Press of Mississippi, 2017) and has published many articles on neoliberalism and Chinese film industry, hip hop culture, Sinophone music, rock 'n' roll film, documentary and transcultural media production. Dr. Xiao also served as producer on TV series, documentary projects, and a narrative feature film. She holds visiting professorships at many international universities, sits on a variety of editorial boards, and serves as reviewer for important academic journals, presses, grants, and awards. She has been actively involved in a number of international film festivals, serving as judge, programmer, and on advisory committee, and has also been extensively interviewed and featured at many national and international news and media outlets.

Markus Pope is an experienced software architect and founder of Code Scientists, LLC, where he serves as Chief Scientist. With nearly four decades in the industry, he has applied his expertise across a broad range of domains, from medical devices and enterprise platforms to AI-enhanced systems and embedded technologies. Markus holds professional certifications from Harvard Medical School and MIT in AI and data science, along with advanced Python programming credentials (PCPP1, PCAP, PCEP). Throughout his career, Markus has contributed to projects involving real-time ECG classification algorithms, wireless protocol analysis, and secure firmware for FDA-regulated devices. His work also includes web-based diagnostic platforms, document management systems, and data visualization tools, leveraging technologies such as C++, Python, Flutter, OpenCV, and TensorFlow. He brings a thoughtful and pragmatic approach to emerging technologies like generative AI, using them as tools to enhance human understanding and design better systems. Markus is also a published author of several programming books, a former academic advisor, and a continuing advocate for responsible innovation in software development.

Dr. Idalis Villanueva Alarcón is Chair and Professor in the Department of Engineering Education in the Herbert Wertheim College of Engineering. A White House presidential PECASE awardee and an American Society of Engineering Fellow, she has led multiple pioneering efforts in engineering education including multimodal methods in engineering education using sensor technologies and biophysiological tools, hidden curriculum, mentoring, active learning, professional identity, among others. She is a renowned national and international leader in engineering education earning her multiple accolades and honors through professional organizations such as the National Academy of Engineering, IEEE, and ASEE. She integrates her multiple experiences as a Chemical Engineering, Biological Engineer, Analytical Cell Biologist, and Engineering Education Researcher to tackle complex engineering education problems across the learner life span.

Dr. Stephan N. Kory is an Associate Professor of Chinese. He has held visiting teaching positions at Tunghai University (ROC), Southwest Jiaotong University (PRC), Reed College, Swarthmore College, and the College of Charleston; along with research fellowships at the International Consortium for Research in the Humanities (IKGF Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg) and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (Beijing). Author of several research articles, encyclopedia entries, and reviews dealing with medieval Chinese literature, religion, and political history, his first book, Technicians and Artisans of Heaven-and-Earth (Brill), will be out later this year. Focusing on imperial memories of diviners, physicians, and craftsmen in mid-medieval China, the book argues that these practitioners were central players in the establishment of medieval dynasties and in the maintenance of imperial power. He is also co-editor of the forthcoming IKGF Handbook of Divination and Prognostication in China, Part 2: Techniques. Dr. Kory teaches courses on Classical Chinese language and on ancient and medieval Chinese literature and culture. He is an active member of several editorial boards and selection committees; and he has participated in, facilitated, and organized several international and national academic conferences, both here in the US and in Europe.

dhq:abstract.p: This article introduces True Digital Poiesis (TDP), a conceptual pedagogical framework and proposed interface design for engaging generative AI in the Humanities. Drawing on experiential learning theory and grounded in the humanistic preoccupation with alterity — the otherness of history — TDP proposes the use of AI to simulate premodern events while foregrounding the active interpretive effort involved in constructing the past. The framework envisions the design of a digital prompt-builder, the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS), and a structured critical review process, both of which are designed to support student engagement with the complexities of historical construction. In presenting the theoretical foundation, practical applications, and interface design of TDP, this article argues that precise and responsible use of AI in historical simulation — ranging from non-immersive to fully immersive simulative modes — requires a systematic, embodied method for engaging the alterity of the past. As a conceptual proposal grounded in hermeneutic theory and experiential learning research, TDP is presented here as a framework whose empirical evaluation through classroom implementation and outcome assessment is a primary objective of ongoing and future research.

dhq:teaser.p: This article introduces True Digital Poiesis, a conceptual framework and interface design that uses generative AI to simulate the premodern past while training students to true their simulations to the historical record.

div.head: 1. Introduction
div.p:
The educational potential of computer simulations has long been recognized within the field of experiential learning
. Yet with the growing technological power driving simulations comes epistemological risk with respect to their accuracy. When simulations are used to reconstruct or represent the past, they engage the persistent challenge of the latter’s alterity, the fundamental differences between remote historical subjects and the contemporary world. As philosophers Hans-Georg Gadamer and Paul Ricœur have argued in different ways, historical understanding is always mediated by present-day assumptions; representations of the past are not transparent windows but constructed interpretations. To address the tensions between present and past, this paper proposes True Digital Poiesis (TDP) as a methodological framework and simulative method. TDP seeks to harness the experiential learning power of generative AI simulations while introducing rigorous structures for critical engagement, revision, and historical accountability. We argue that TDP — which employs a combination of traditional humanities methods (such as source-based inquiry and iterative revision) and novel digital tools — provides a systematic approach to embedding humanistic reflection within AI-driven learning environments.

By emphasizing poiesis — the act of making — as a creative and interpretive process of understanding the past, the TDP method teaches students to generate historical simulations as well as to actively negotiate the meanings, omissions, and perspectives that shape them. Crucially, TDP frames this act of making as something qualitatively distinct from other forms of student-AI interaction: It is not the use of AI as an answer machine or as a writing assistant, but as a medium of structured historical construction in which the learner’s interpretive choices are continuously foregrounded, tested, and revised. This article presents the theoretical grounding of the framework, its technical and pedagogical components, and its broader implications for digital learning in the humanities.

div.head: 2. Alterity and the Digital Simulation of the Past
div.p: The concept of alterity — the appreciation of the otherness of the past — has long stood at the heart of humanistic inquiry. Whether in historical writing, literary analysis, or the study of art and culture, scholars have sought to engage and interpret the distance that separates us from past worlds and historically remote cultures. This distance places significant constraints on historical representation. To claim to see the past wie es eigentlich gewesen (as it really was, as historian Leopold von Ranke famously put it in the early nineteenth century) has long since come to be widely understood as an illusion. As R.G. Collingwood argued in The Idea of History (1946), historical knowledge is not the passive recovery of past facts but the active re-enactment of past thought in the historian’s own mind — an insight that anticipates the constructivist turn in historiography and speaks directly to the designed interactivity of TDP. Hayden White’s Metahistory (1973) further demonstrated that historical accounts are shaped by narrative forms and rhetorical choices that are irreducibly present-oriented: Representations of past events, figures, and systems are always mediated by language, by interests and preferences, and by the narrative frameworks of the present. Historical accounts, as the mere subtitle of Stefan Berger’s 2022 historiographical study How Historical Theory Shapes Historical Practice announces, tell us as much about the interests and needs of the present as they do about the content of the past.

The humanities must take seriously the imperative to negotiate alterity; to account both for the ultimate irrecoverability of the past as it really was and for the pressing immediacy of the concerns of the modern interpretive frameworks through which the past is being accessed.

Within the critical hermeneutic tradition, Hans-Georg Gadamer has argued that historical understanding is never a simple recovery of what was, but always a dialogical process, a fusion of […] horizons supposedly existing in themselves . In this fusion, present and past engage and transform each other. The engagement with the past is not an act of assimilation but of negotiation, a mutual reshaping in which, as Gadamer puts it, understanding involves guarding against overhastily assimilating the past to our own expectations of meaning. Only then can we listen to tradition in a way that permits its own meaning to be heard . Also in the critical hermeneutic tradition, Paul Ricœur addresses the necessity of resisting the violence of interpretation — or the wholesale adoption of the past in the interest of some compelling present agenda — on the one hand; and the possible redundance of an interpretative approach that would naively (mis)take the past as just another version of the present, on the other . The insights of Gadamer and Ricœur applied to the present moment make clear that any procedure for digital simulation — especially those with a high degree of audiovisual realism — must be designed not to collapse or flatten our distance from the past overhastily (contrast , but to highlight and sustain the plenitude of its alterity.

The term poiesis, in our use, reflects the tension between creative construction and interpretive fidelity. A substantive form of the Ancient Greek poieîn — to make, to bring into being — this term foregrounds the active role we play in shaping the past. What makes poiesis the right concept here, rather than merely iteration or construction, is its implication of purposeful, skilled making: the craftsman who shapes material toward a form that did not previously exist but that is constrained by the properties of the material itself. In TDP, that material is the historical record — primary and secondary sources whose alterity resists arbitrary reconfiguration. The poietic act in TDP is not arbitrary creativity but responsible making: a process in which students or researchers negotiate between the demands of historical evidence and the inevitably present-oriented frameworks they bring to it. This is what distinguishes TDP from other structured prompting approaches: It is not enough to produce a well-formed prompt or a plausible narrative; the student must account for the interpretive choices embedded in each step of the construction.

Generative artificial intelligence raises the stakes for this kind of poietic engagement precisely because of its power to simulate historical scenes with persuasive realism. The rise of generative AI introduces a new and urgent complication to our interpretive landscape. With tools ever more capable of producing fully immersive, richly detailed audiovisual simulations at scale, the temptation to mistake the fake for the real has never been greater. Large language models (LLMs), trained on vast corpora of human-generated text, generate outputs by predicting statistically likely continuations of prompts — they do not know history in the way a trained historian does. This distinction has significant implications for historical simulation. LLMs may produce historically plausible-sounding narratives that are factually inaccurate, anachronistic, or that systematically favor perspectives overrepresented in their training data . The phenomenon popularly known as hallucination — the confident generation of false or fabricated information — arises from this statistical mode of text generation: The model produces what is likely, not necessarily what is true. Moreover, training corpora reflect the biases and gaps of the historical record itself, which skews toward literate, elite, and Western perspectives. A simulation of a medieval peasant uprising, for instance, may draw more heavily on chroniclers’ accounts than on archaeological or social-historical evidence, simply because the former dominate the available textual data. The persuasive power of simulations produced by generative AI as a potentially superintelligent tool risks sidelining the critical sensibilities for engaging otherness that the humanities must cultivate. If seeing is believing, then any simulated past risks being mistaken for the recovered past unless the learner is trained to recognize and account for the structured processes behind its generation.

To counteract the risk of remaking the past in the image of the present (either violently or redundantly, recalling the Scylla and Charybdis of Ricœur) the True Digital Poiesis method emphasizes the iterative, reflective nature of historical simulation. It does not propose a single definitive version of events but treats each simulation as a provisional interpretive act, a hypothesis to be tested rather than a product to be consumed. The concept of truing is useful here. In its verbal, mechanical sense, to true something is to bring it into alignment or balance, to make it level, square, and concentric relative to a set of defined criteria . A simulation, in TDP terms, is never absolutely true — this would be to repeat the illusion of Ranke — but it can be trued relative to the complexity and rigor of the criteria against which it is assessed. This concept of truing provides an epistemologically honest metaphor for what TDP asks students to do: not to recover the past, but to calibrate their representations of it as carefully and self-consciously as possible. It also provides a productive organizing principle for the method’s iterative structure, as we describe below. The educational challenge remains never completely to collapse the tension between our participation in the past and present, but to hold it open so that the learner is always situated both within and at a distance from the simulated events.

The connection between these hermeneutic concepts and the specific steps of the TDP workflow — described in full in Section 4 below — is worth making explicit here. The initial population of the 5W1H (i.e. who, what, when, where, why, how?) framework (Step 1) represents the learner’s pre-understanding: the horizon of assumptions, knowledge, and interpretive frameworks they bring to the encounter with the past. The AI-generated simulation (Step 2) represents the first articulation of that pre-understanding in narrative form — a moment in which the learner’s inputs are rendered visible as a constructed object. The critical review step (Step 3), in which the student discovers discrepancies between the simulation and their sources, represents the kind of productive dissonance that Gadamer describes as the encounter with the genuinely other: the moment at which the past resists assimilation. The revision step, in which the student adjusts their inputs for the purpose of regenerating the simulation, represents the reshaping of understanding that constitutes the fusion of horizons — not a dissolution of the distance between past and present, but a more critically aware negotiation of it. In this sense, TDP is not merely a workflow that uses AI; it is a hermeneutic method that uses AI as one of its instruments.

Our method undertakes this through iterative cycles of revision in which learners assess the coherence of their simulations, cross-check historical accuracy against primary and secondary sources, and identify anachronisms or assumptions that may distort the past. The steps involved in producing and reviewing a simulation as something being made remain front and center in the workflow as a practice to be cultivated and appreciated as much as the overall quality of the simulations produced. In a classroom scenario, the role of the instructor correspondingly shifts, in part, from judging based on their own subject matter expertise the correctness of the content of the produced simulation, to keeping the students’ focus as much on the steps they are taking to produce the simulation as on the simulation content itself. A critical awareness of the inevitable codependence of TDP steps and resulting output is thereby inculcated. The fusion of generative AI with a self-aware and hands-on approach to the past thus leads — to the degree TDP can be foregrounded and cultivated as learning practice — to a dynamic poietic engagement that keeps alterity at the center of a digital pedagogy that is both creative and historically aware.

div.head: 3. Digital Simulations as Experiential Learning
div.p: The hermeneutic insight that simulations of the past must be designed to sustain rather than collapse alterity, that they must keep the learner simultaneously within and at a distance from the events being reconstructed, has a natural and productive counterpart in the theory of experiential learning. If Gadamer and Ricœur tell us how to engage the past responsibly, the tradition of experiential learning research tells us why the simulative mode of engagement is worth taking seriously in the first place: because it is precisely this mode — the active, iterative, hands-on encounter with constructed scenarios — that research consistently identifies as among the most cognitively and motivationally powerful available to learners (wildman_etal 2017). The challenge, as the following discussion makes clear, is to bring these two bodies of insight — the hermeneutic and the experiential — into alignment, so that the experienced power of simulation does not come at the expense of the critical distance that humanistic inquiry requires.

In his seminal work, Experiential Learning: Experience as the Source of Learning and Development (1984), David Kolb identifies simulation as a means of enabling learners to engage in active experimentation, receive immediate feedback, and refine their understanding through iterative practice . Simulations, in this sense, are not simply illustrative; they are generative tools that catalyze learning by doing. Building on Kolb’s framework, recent scholarship has explored the power of immersive and interactive technologies — particularly virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and now generative artificial intelligence (AI) — to expand the reach and intensity of experiential learning across disciplines. Studies by , , , , , , , and (marougkas_etal, 2023) have emphasized in different ways the motivational and cognitive benefits of immersive experiential learning environments. Technological developments increasingly allow learners to engage in experiential learning with complex material in a fully immersive, multisensory (i.e. multimodal), emotionally resonant, and often collaborative manner.

While maintaining its stake in hermeneutic reflection and experiential learning, TDP also takes its place within a landscape of simulation-based historical pedagogy grounded in the digital humanities that predates AI-driven approaches and provides important precedents for assessing what is genuinely new about them. Jeremiah McCall’s work on the Historical Problem Space framework — which conceptualizes historical simulations as structured possibility-spaces in which different inputs produce different historical outcomes — and on gaming the past more broadly demonstrates how video games function as environments in which students engage with the constraints and possibilities of historical agency. Mark Carnes’s Reacting to the Past method (2014) uses elaborate role-playing simulations to immerse students in historical debates, with documented effects on student engagement and historical thinking. These approaches share TDP’s core conviction that constructing and inhabiting simulated versions of the past is a powerful pedagogical mode. TDP extends this tradition into the domain of generative AI, where the simulation is not pre-authored by a game designer or instructor but co-constructed by the student and the AI — a configuration that raises the stakes for critical scaffolding, since the AI’s outputs may carry an authority that a student-authored text does not. The digital humanities tradition reinforces and extends this conviction: Stephen Ramsay’s concept of algorithmic criticism suggests that computational tools can serve as instruments of interpretive inquiry rather than merely as efficiency aids — a principle that TDP extends into the domain of historical simulation.

For all its promise, the application of simulations for the purposes of experiential learning in the humanities has often lagged behind its use in technical and professional fields . Part of the reason likely lies in the humanities’ emphasis on interpretation, ambiguity, and critical reflection — of the hermeneutic kind considered in the previous section, for example — qualities that can be difficult to reconcile with the immersive realism of simulation environments. Humanities scholars understandably balk in the face of the risk that students will mistake engagement with high-fidelity reproductions for understanding, simulated presence for real historical experience. This problem is particularly acute in the context of generative AI where outputs can be so convincing in their audiovisual verisimilitude that they risk short-circuiting the critically self-reflective distance essential to humanistic inquiry.

True Digital Poiesis proposes to resolve this tension between the humanities’ commitment to critically reflective distance and the immersive pull of AI-generated simulation, not by slowing down or stepping back from the technology, but by building the structures of humanistic reflection directly into the simulation workflow, into the way prompts are constructed, into the criteria by which outputs are assessed, and into the iterative cycle of revision through which each simulation is progressively trued. Rather than positioning generative AI as an end-product tool, the TDP method treats it as part of an iterative, critical method that combines simulation with structured research, embodied interaction, and systematic review. In this way, TDP seeks to reclaim AI-generated simulation as a vehicle for active learning on humanistic terms: through guided construction, embedded revision, and self-reflective interpretation. Just as Kolb emphasized the cyclical nature of experiential learning — moving from concrete experience to reflection, conceptualization, and experimentation — TDP designs a parallel process for engaging with the past in a hermeneutically informed way. Learners construct simulations based on their research, test and revise those simulations in response to inconsistencies, anachronisms, and other shortcomings, and reflect critically on the assumptions embedded in the simulative process. The result is a dynamic, hands-on encounter with historical records and artefacts that preserves the rigor of humanistic inquiry while embracing the power of new technologies.

div.head: 4. The True Digital Poiesis Method
div.p: The TDP Method is a structured pedagogical framework designed to harness the power of generative AI while embedding it within the interpretive and critical methods of the humanities. At its core, TDP is an iterative and source-based simulation-building process that involves students in constructing historically aware event simulations while constantly engaging with the alterity of the past as they are constructing and simulating. TDP consists of three primary steps:

div.p: Each step is guided by the principle of poiesis — a deliberate, creative, and critically informed process of making. The Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS), described in detail in the following section, is an interface implementation, currently in design development, that gives three-dimensional embodied form to this method. In its current classroom-tested implementation, the method is realized through a two-dimensional Questions Grid that guides students through the 5W1H framework using a standard web-based interface:

div.head: Step 1: Structured Research and Prompt Construction
div.p: The initial step of the TDP Method centers on embedding traditional scholarly practices — such as the use of primary and secondary sources, coherent narrative structure, and causal reasoning — within the very architecture of generative AI prompts. Students begin by populating a digital prompt-building tool (currently the Questions Grid, later the ECS) based on the classical 5W1H method: Who? What? When? Where? Why? and How? These questions recommend themselves as a principled framework for historical inquiry because they correspond to the basic categories through which historians structure causal narrative: actors, actions, localities, temporalities, and teleological and instrumental causalities. Crucially, these are also interpretive categories. To sort evidence under the heading why? is already to make a claim about causation that the historical record may complicate. This is the insight that Drucker develops through her distinction between data and capta : What we treat as raw information is always already shaped by the interpretive choices involved in its capture and formatting. The fields of critical making and critical code studies extend this point to the design of tools themselves, arguing that the assumptions embedded in a tool’s architecture are never neutral — an insight that TDP endeavors to take into account by making the (revisable) defining criteria associated with each 5W1H question a transparent component of its method, as further explained below.

Each of the six questions of the TDP method is linked in the prompt-building tool to specific criteria set by the instructor, such as the backstories of historical actors, the temporal and geographical specificities of events, the motivations and mechanics according to which historical events are assumed to play out, etc. Students assemble information from textual, visual, and audiovisual sources corresponding to the criteria for each question, thus grounding their simulations in historical research. This process of assembling and categorizing sources is itself a poietic act: The student is not merely retrieving information but actively building a structured representation of the past shapes what the AI can produce.

div.head: Step 2: Generative Simulation
div.p: Once the Questions Grid is complete, students use it to generate a narrative simulation using a large language model (LLM). The output is a simulation — a narrative account or dramatized historical scene — that reflects the content of the prompt. Criteria can be scaled to require research that leads to simple simulations with basic information or more detailed simulations requiring greater precision and detail. The aim is not to produce a definitive account of the past but a provisional simulation that can be interrogated, tested, and refined — a hypothesis, in Collingwood’s terms, to be submitted to historical criticism .

The use of the term simulation for text-based AI generation may seem to require some justification, since simulation typically implies a dynamic, multi-state model. We use the term deliberately, in alignment with the broader tradition of historical simulation studies , to indicate that the AI-generated narrative represents a specific configuration of historical variables — actors, places, times, causes — that can be altered and re-run. What makes this configurability epistemologically significant is precisely that adjusting the student’s prompt inputs produces a different rendering of the same historical moment. The simulation is not a fixed account but a structured representation of a possible past, subject to revision. In this sense, a screen-based narrative output functions as a simulation in the meaningful sense the term requires because it externalizes a set of interpretive choices — choices that can be identified, interrogated, and revised. The broader tradition of historical simulation pedagogy (wildman_etal 2017) has established this usage; the specific contribution of TDP is to make the configurability of those choices — and therefore the revisability of the outputs they generate — explicit and pedagogically foregrounded through the 5W1H framework.

Current LLMs perform unevenly across historical domains, tending to generate more plausible and detailed outputs for periods and places heavily represented in their English-language training data — medieval Western Europe, for instance — than for periods and cultures underrepresented within it: e.g. sub-Saharan African medieval history, pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, or pre-modern East Asian contexts in which the primary sources are not in English. This unevenness is not a disqualifying limitation of the TDP method; rather, its review step (Step 3) is precisely designed to make such imbalances visible and correctable. Students working on underrepresented historical contexts will find that their simulations require more intensive revision and that the review step surfaces limitations traceable to the generative AI’s configuration and training and TDP’s own question criteria rather than to the historical record — a distinction that is itself a significant lesson in the critical use of AI.

div.head: Step 3: Iterative Review and Revision
div.p: The final step of the TDP method is paramount: The simulation undergoes structured critical review. Students analyze the simulation output according to three key criteria:

list.item: Internal Consistency: Are the actions, actors, temporalities, localities, and causal structures coherent within the framework of the prompt?
Source Accuracy: How faithfully does the simulation reflect the primary and secondary sources cited in the prompt construction?
Historical Plausibility: What inaccuracies, inconsistencies, or anachronisms have emerged, and how can they best be addressed?

div.p: Learners then revise the information in the digital prompt builder based on their critical findings, with a view to re-running the simulation with the expectation of a better result. Each iteration is undertaken on the understanding that it can bring students into closer contact with both the historical material and the interpretive assumptions with which they have arranged it. The process of truing the simulation — bringing it into closer alignment with the criteria and sources that define it — is itself the primary educational experience, not the means to any finished product.

When a student’s iterative review reveals that the LLM consistently fails to represent certain historical perspectives regardless of what sources are supplied, this is not a failure of TDP but a boundary condition that TDP is designed to make visible. An LLM trained on a corpus that systematically underrepresents non-Western, non-elite, or non-literate historical actors will tend to produce narratives that reflect those biases even when the student’s prompt includes corrective sources. Making this limitation legible — teaching students to recognize and name it as a feature of the tool rather than of the historical record — is itself a significant pedagogical outcome of the review step.

div.head: 5. Academic Context and Pedagogical Application
div.p: The TDP method is currently being developed, with support from the University of Florida Artificial Intelligence and Informatics Research Institute, in MEM 3510: Engineering the European Middle Ages, an undergraduate course at the University of Florida. This course serves as the primary site of prototype development for the TDP methodology and its supporting tools. Within this learning environment, students engage with historical materials through a structured, research-based process that culminates in the generation and critical scrutiny of AI-enhanced simulations of premodern events.

The workflow is currently based on a simple Questions Grid (Figure 2 below) that guides students through the 5W1H framework. For each of these fundamental questions and its respective criteria, students populate the grid with specific content drawn from primary and secondary sources. This includes textual passages (composed by the students themselves or other scholars), image references, audio files, etc. Information must be duly cited according to the standards set down in the prompt criteria. Once the grid is completed, the data is used to prompt a large language model (LLM), which generates a non-immersive (i.e. screen-based) narrative simulation (definitions of the different immersive scales of VR are provided by . These simulations vary in form — from dramatized accounts of historical episodes to imagined dialogues, ritual descriptions, or political negotiations — but all reflect the source material and question criteria for the 5W1H framework as set down in the grid. In this way, the simulation becomes a kind of testable hypothesis, produced not merely for its aesthetic or narrative value, but as an instrument of historical thinking. Following generation, simulations are subjected to a structured critical review. In the current working version of TDP, students have completed this review using the Track Changes feature in Microsoft Word, inserting comments, corrections, and reflections directly into their AI-generated narrative simulations.

figure.head: TDP Questions Grid
figure.figDesc: Blank Questions Grid template with six columns — Who?, What?, Where?, When?, How?, and Why? — each listing instructor-defined criteria above an empty row for student entries, followed by instructions to cite at least six primary or secondary sources per question.

div.head: Example of Student Work using the Questions Grid
div.p: For an example of the TDP workflow as it currently operates in the classroom with the two-dimensional Questions Grid as the prompt-building interface, consider the following example drawn from actual student work in MEM 3510. In Module 5 of MEM 3510, a student group with the name The Last Romans was assigned to simulate an episode involving medieval warfare technology. They chose to reconstruct the Siege of Orléans of 1428–1429, centering their simulation on the intersection of traditional siege warfare and the emerging gunpowder weapons — cannons, hand-held firearms, fireboats — that marked a turning point in the Hundred Years’ War. Their Questions Grid (Figure 3) populates all six 5W1H columns: situating Joan of Arc within the political and theological context of late medieval France, locating the siege within Orléans’s strategic geography as the northernmost city still loyal to the French crown, and encoding the students’ research judgment that gunpowder weapons — particularly on the French side — were a defining feature of this phase of the conflict.

table.head: The Last Romans’ Completed Question Grid with Sources

row.cell: Joan of Arc was born in 1412 in Domremy, France. No one could have expected this young peasant girl would become one of France’s most iconic historical figures, standing high as a Patron Saint and national hero comparable to the French on the levels of Napoleon or De Gaulle (#1, Joan of Arc: The Image of Female Heroism). Northern France had come under foreign English occupation, and as the Hundred Year’s War continued to rage on, she claimed to have heard divinely inspired messages from holy Christian visions and voices. (Image credit: Joan of Arc: A Military Leader). She identified these voices as saints and called on the fighting French to keep pushing out the English conquerors. Her most legendary contribution to the Hundred Year’s War came at the Siege of Orleans, where her arrival was marked by banners and armor which she, a woman in medieval Europe, was bold enough to don. (#2, Siege Warfare during the Hundred Years War). The inspiration she gave to the French army in Orleans brought them great strength and confidence, allowing them to push out bold attacks that ended the siege within days. (Image credit: Battle of Crécy). In this narrative, one French soldier, Jacques and Louis, fictional characters inspired by the real fighting men of France during the Siege of Orleans, stand strong and live through the horrors of war. Jacques’ survivorship comes with a renounced sense of nationalist pride in France after their successive victories, inspired by Joan of Arc’s heroic presence. Jacques and Louis represent the early national spirit of the French people as they fought to secure their freedom. (#3, Page not found | Taylor & Francis Group). His role in the army as an archer, specifically trained as a soldier to fire arrows from crossbows, makes him a powerful and precise shooter.

(Image Source: Google Images) The Hundred Years’ War between France and England originated as a dispute between two nobles and their respective claims to the throne. Philip of Valois from France, who was backed by the French nobility, did not recognize the claim of Edward III from England (History Mapped Out, 2024). While France allied with Scotland, they mounted an attack on English-held Gascony at the south of France. This marked the start of the Hundred Years’ War. (#1 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VO0ylL3JRKk) (Image Source: Google Images) The Hundred Years’ War was marked by a series of decisive battles that shaped Europe's political landscape. The English secured early victories at Crécy (1346) and Poitiers (1356), thanks to their skilled longbowmen and disciplined infantry. However, momentum later shifted toward the French under figures such as Joan of Arc, whose faith and strategy inspired the French to reclaim key territories, including Orléans in 1429. These turning points not only demonstrated the evolving art of warfare but also reflected the rise of nationalism in both kingdoms (History Mapped Out, 2024). (Source Image: Google Images) The Siege of Orléans became one of the defining moments of the Hundred Years’ War. English and Burgundian forces launched an assault on the French city of Orléans, a strategic gateway to southern France and one of the last strongholds loyal to Charles VII (Gillum, 2022). After months of siege, the city’s defenders were struggling to hold out. The arrival of Joan of Arc in April 1429 changed the course of the conflict. Her presence revitalized French morale and inspired a series of daring attacks that forced the English to retreat in May 1429. (#2 https://www.ebs co.com/researchstarters/history/s iege-orleans

Orléans is a city in the north of France located on the Loire River. It was notable in the period for it being the northernmost city in France which was still aligned with the French crown. Most of the rest of the north was controlled by the English and allies of the English such as the Burgundians. (#1 Jeanne d'Arc (1412-1431) ) (Photo Credit: Siege of 1429 ) The location of Orléans was essential to the time period because of its significance as the capital of the Orléans Duchy. The dukes of Orléans were also notable leaders of a political faction called the Armagnacs which were loyal to the uncrowned Charles VII. Beyond that, the city served as a barrier of sorts from the English-loyal north to the French-loyal south and protected the French area from exposure to the English.
(Photo Credit: Jeanne d'Arc (1412- 1431)) There were various aspects of the physicality of Orléans which predisposed it to this warfare. For one, the aforementioned loyalty barriers of Orléans and the psychological blow that conquering the city would give to the already weakened French. More than that, the geography of the area also predisposed the city for battle. The location of the city on the Loire River allowed for a physical barrier which if overtaken would easily allow the siege of the rest of France. Anticipating this siege on the River and Bridge, the French fortified the Les Tourelles gatehouse which was located in the water. This further protected the river from weaponry of warfare such as cannons which previously would have easily taken over the weakened bridge. (#2 Siege of Orleans | Sevenswords) (Photo Credit: Significant Battles in 'Henry the Sixth Part One' | Theatre Production Archive | University of Waterloo)

The time period of the Battle of Orleans, and greater 100 Years War marked a turning point in the tools of warfare for the time. (Photo Credit: Cry Havoc: Siege of Orléans)) It was significant for tying together the traditional tools of Siege warfare along with the emerging weapons of warfare such as gunpowder artillery. (#1 EBSCO | Siege of Orléans) The battle took place from October 12, 1428 to May 8, 1429 and was placed within the larger context of the 100 Years War which took place from 1337–1453. (Photo Credit: The Origins of the Hundred Years War - Historic UK) This battle took place at an essential turning point within the war. If the French city of Orleans would have fallen, it most likely would have meant that France as a country would have entirely fallen to the English due to their dominance in the war previously, demonstrated in their victories such as Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356, and Agincourt in 1415. The larger war was a story of English victories so the French’s victory was essential to their survival as a nation. (#2 Joan of Arc: a military leader | DeVries, Kelly ) and (#3 The Maiden of France: A Brief Overview of Joan of Arc and the Siege of Orléans | Cam Rea) Finally, this battle was so essential to the war because of the timing of the battle itself. As previously mentioned, the war was heavily dominated by English successes so the French victory was essential for French morale. Without the victory at Orléans, the French, if not conquered through warfare, likely would have surrendered to the English due to the hopelessness experienced. Through the blockade, supplies were being held from the French living in Orleans, causing many residents to starve, or not have essential materials for living. (Photo Credit: CannonsFiring At The Walls During The Siege Of Orleans) Through this victory, the French secured a turning point in the war and allowed their people to hang on. (#4 Siege of Orléans | Britannica

(Image Source: Google Images) The Hundred Years’ War brought about a change in warfare and military strategy. Infantrymen and longbowmen became essential for the English, especially famously at the battle of Agincourt (Green, 2014). This changed meant that warfare was stepping away from knights and towards employing mercenaries and peasantry in both France and England. These shifts altered the structure of armies and redefined social roles in medieval society, as commoners began to play a larger part in national defense. The evolution of tactics and technology during this period laid the groundwork for the end of feudal-style warfare in Europe. (#1 https://tinyurl.co m/mwykaj53) (Source: Google Images) Created in the 12th century by the Welsh, the longbow became pivotal for the English during the Hundred Years’ War (Lyons, C). Longbows were about 6 feet long, and longbowmen needed to apply 80 to 120 pounds of tension. They were loaded faster than crossbows, and because they were vertical, archers could be placed closer together than with crossbows. Mandatory military training in England helped improve the discipline of troops and also improve training with longbows. ( #2 https://tinyurl.com/mrkdba6y ) (Image Source: Google Images) On the other hand, the French more widely adopted gunpowder weapons. Although in the earlier battles in the Hundred Years' War the longbowmen dominated, later battles proved successful for the gunpowder-weapon-wielding Frenchmen (DeVries, 2010). These weapons are often referenced to be cannons. Beyond the adoption of actual gunpowder weapons, the success lay in France’s investment in organizing the duties of cannoneers, increasing pay, and establishing officers. (#3 https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315249230)

Joan of Arc’s involvement with the Hundred year’s war between France and England, some scholar and historians call Joan of Arc’s relief of Orléans. This term refers to the pivotal event in the Siege of Orléans in the Hundred Year’s War. Joan of Arc was involved with this war and specifically this battle/siege because she had divine intervention/a vision (some even argue voices) telling her to lead help/rescue Orléans and also that she was basically sent by God to save/help the French in their efforts to win the war. Joan acted the way she did because she believed she was sent by God to help the French, which lead to her leading the French army in the battle of Orléans and they won this battle. According to a dissertation done by a student at Bosie State University it states, Joan convinced the leading French theologians and France’s future king that the Divine had sent her; they in turn, provided her with armor to wear and placed a force of four thousand men under her command. She set off towards Orléans soon after, carrying a white banner depicting Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and two angels (#1 Bosie State University Joan of Arc Dissertation (Joan of Arc Carrying the Banner) England’s why was the main cause for the Siege of Orléans, and it was because they wanted to quickly end this war. But this siege did not go in their favor. France’s why for this event is multi-faceted. They reacted the way they did in this siege because had a lot to do with Joan of Arc. Joan of Arc touched the French leaders and convinced them to let her help them. During this siege the Joan arrived in the Orléans with thousands of men from the French army. Lastly according to EBSCO, While the army leaders discussed plans, Joan mixed with the troops and citizens of Orléans. On May 4, the comte de Dunois attacked the English garrison in the church of St. Loup east of Orléans. Joan joined the fray and was so effective in rallying French troops that she was assigned a part in the next attack. On May 6, the French committed about 4,000 troops to assaulting English positions at the south end of the Orléans bridge. In a day of fighting, the French captured the fortified monastery of Augustine, although the English held out in the fortified towers on the bridge itself. Joan insisted on renewing the attack on May 7 and repeatedly rallied the French until a complex night attack (including a fireboat) overwhelmed the English. The recovery of the bridge made the rest of the siege nearly meaningless. The English army challenged the French to battle on May 8, then marched away after the French declined. The siege was over, and Orléans gave the credit to the peasant girl. In the ensuing days, the French proceeded against the smaller English outposts on the Loire. Joan persuaded the French commanders to attack a 5,000-man English relief army on the march near Patay. The English army, surprised, was destroyed as an organized force (#2 Siege of Orleans EBSCO) So, Joan of Arc was a big part of France’s why for this siege/battle.

div.p: The narrative simulation generated from this grid — The Siege of Orléans: Voices of Faith and Fire — places named fictional characters inside the historical event with dialogue, sensory detail, and dramatic stakes. Among the French troops marching with Joan are Jacques, a crossbow archer, and Louis, his companion designated as a cannoneer, through whom the simulation renders the shift in medieval warfare from the chivalric rhythms of armored combat toward the psychological and material force of gunpowder. The simulation follows the two soldiers through Joan’s arrival in Orléans on April 29, 1429, the assault on the English stronghold at Les Tourelles on May 7, and the lifting of the siege the following dawn (the AI-generated narrative is included in this article as Appendix 1).

The students’ Track Changes review (Figure 4) conducts Step 3 of the TDP workflow directly on this simulation, and the annotations reveal something the method predicts: that the AI’s output, however fluent, systematically reorients the historical material toward the statistically familiar. One student changed Louis’s original designation from swordsman to cannoneer, noting that the revision was intended to highlight the importance and prevalence of gunpowder weapons on France’s side of the latter half of the Hundred Years’ War — a correction grounded in what the grid’s sources had established and the AI had quietly set aside. The same student then removed a reference attributing cannon fire to the English as well, because the sources placed more emphasis on France’s use and adoption of cannons, where the grid had encoded an asymmetry between the two sides’ weapons profiles, the AI had smoothed it into symmetry. Another student adjusted Joan’s dialogue and a soldier’s affirmation of faith to better reflect, in the annotation’s words, Christian values as a Frenchman of the time would think — a correction in which the AI’s generically heroic register is identified as insufficiently historically estranged and revised toward the specific theological idiom of late medieval French piety. This is the encounter with alterity that TDP’s review step is designed to produce: not an abstract awareness that the past was different, but a concrete, comparative confrontation with the differences between what the sources encode and what the model generates.

figure.head: The Last Roman’s Critical Review
figure.figDesc: A word document with student comments indentifying issues with the AI's output

div.p: The group’s written analysis of the AI output identifies this gap in terms that echo the article’s own theoretical framework. The AI, they observe, did not take into full effect all of the information from our questions grid, and its failure to capture the tone and interpretive orientation of the grid's source material could be considered a hallucination — a formulation that intuitively grasps the distinction between what a language model produces statistically and what a historically grounded prompt actually demands. In Gadamerian terms, the students have encountered the moment at which the simulation resists assimilation to their own horizon: The AI has rendered the past in a present-oriented image, and the review step has made that rendering visible as a construction to be corrected rather than a recovery to be accepted.

One further feature of the submission is worth noting. Despite the cannoneer designation introduced in Louis’s first appearance, he dies sword in hand two paragraphs later — an inconsistency the revision did not catch, and that a further iteration of the TDP cycle would need to address. This is not a failure of the method but a demonstration of one of its central claims: that a single cycle of review and revision is rarely sufficient to true a simulation fully, and that the iterative structure of TDP exists precisely to make successive incompletions visible and correctable. The grid, simulation, and annotated review together constitute not a finished product but a documented, iterable artifact — a record not merely of what the students produced but of how far, in this iteration, they have trued it.

div.head: 6. True Digital Poiesis and Event Cruncher Stylus Prototype Reference Architecture
div.p: The TDP method is currently being extended toward fully immersive (bonsu_etal, 2025) audio-visual simulations of premodern events using generative AI tools for audio, imagery, and video. This more ambitious simulative goal involves transforming the two-dimensional Questions Grid currently used for narrative simulations into a three-dimensional interactive digital tool called the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS) (Figure 5). The ECS is a proposed interface implementation, currently in design development, that gives three-dimensional, embodied form to the three-step TDP method.

Evidence from the haptic feedback literature suggests that such a multidimensional interface model may offer additional cognitive and pedagogical benefits. The proposed ECS reinforces conceptual distinctions through spatial interaction by mapping questions to distinct manipulable faces of nested three-dimensional solids. This spatial separation is designed to support the development of critical thinking and skills acquisition and to improve cognitive engagement by anchoring abstract reasoning in tactile form. Haptic feedback, and eventually visuo-haptic feedback, may further enhance students’ abilities to conceptualize complex historical relationships by physically reinforcing the separations between temporal, spatial, causal, and agentive dimensions of the six questions .

figure.head: A Static Representation of the Event Cruncher Stylus
figure.figDesc: A static visualization of the Event Cruncher Stylus as nested binary, tetrahedron, cube, and octahedron.

div.p: The ECS design makes use of Platonic solids — three-dimensional geometric forms whose faces are identical regular polygons meeting at identical angles, a property of perfect regularity that makes them uniquely symmetric among all possible polyhedra and that has made them objects of scientific and philosophical fascination from antiquity to the present day . The ECS uses three of the five such forms nested concentrically, mapping questions to distinct faces: The binary at its center represents the distinction between who? and what?; the tetrahedron (four faces) adds the distinctions where? and when?; the cube (six faces) adds the distinctions how? and why?; and the octahedron (eight faces) as the outermost shell serves as the user’s primary interactive control surface. The choice of these forms is motivated by their mathematical regularity, which makes each face of each solid both visually distinct and geometrically equivalent.

The cube, with its six faces arranged in three pairs of opposites, is the component of the ECS that encompasses all six fundamental questions. It does so in the manner of a volumetric Semiotic Square. The latter, developed by linguist A.J. Greimas (1983), is a diagram of logical relations among concepts in which four terms are arranged to make visible three kinds of structural relationships: contradiction (A versus not-A), contrariety (A versus its structural opposite B), and complementarity (A versus what mediates between A and not-B). The diagrams in the next section are correspondingly designed to render explicit the relational architecture that any conceptual field involves but rarely states. In the three-dimensional cube of the ECS, the six questions are arranged so that they stand in analogous relationships of equal, opposite, and adjacent, extending the semiotic structure into three dimensions and giving it a spatial, manipulable form. This design choice reflects the conviction that the six fundamental questions are not merely a checklist but a structured field of relations whose logic should be visible and tangible to the student.

As with the Questions Grid, each question is associated by instructors with defining criteria to guide learners’ research. Each question with its associated criteria corresponds to a face of a Platonic solid functioning as a repository into which corresponding information obtained by learners’ research can be uploaded — or, consistent with the purpose of the ECS as stylus — functioning as a page on which the corresponding information obtained by learners’ research can be written. The transparent octahedron as the outermost solid functions both 1) to serve as a combination digital writing utensil and remote control that the user manipulates (for accessing and editing the criteria and data within and for initiating simulations); and 2) to behave, when a simulation is initiated, like a top that wobbles corresponding to the (im)balance of the data-criteria correspondences within it (the spinning ECS will be visible in the user’s digital field of vision as the simulation occurs). The latter function will allow users to gauge how much fine-tuning their simulation needs (by checking: Are all questions addressed? Has the required number of primary and secondary sources been cited? Does the information provided for each fundamental question consistently align with the question and its criteria?).

Corresponding to its balance, a given simulation will be understood to be true in the verbal sense of the word: to make level, square, balanced, or concentric: bring or restore to a desired mechanical accuracy or form . Edits made to successive iterations of a given ECS digital composition will be tracked and made accessible to learners to be used as part of a structured critical review built into the digital user interface. One of the main purposes of work with the ECS as three-dimensional interactive prompt builder is to offset the role played by visual and audial aspects of the generative AI-based experiential learning by placing greater emphasis on the constructive role played by the tactile sense . In tactile-digital work with the ECS, the main focus falls on the cube which, by incorporating all six basic questions, most closely approximates the linguistic and physical spacetime humanity actually inhabits.

The True Digital Poiesis system is currently implemented as a functional prototype in which the two-dimensional Questions Grid still serves as the primary interface through which students construct their prompts. In this implementation, as we saw in the example above, students populate the grid using a web-based application built with JavaScript, Node.js, and MySQL, then manually transfer the generated prompts into commercial AI platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini to produce their simulations. The three-dimensional, haptic-enabled Event Cruncher Stylus described in this article is an interface design currently in development; it represents the target architecture toward which the system is progressing, not a feature of the tool as presently used in the classroom. Future deployment on the University of Florida’s PubApps hosting service, with integration of AI services powered by HiPerGator and the addition of the fully interactive three-dimensional ECS, version control, multimodal output, and single sign-on authentication, is planned as the next phase of the TDP project.

div.head: 7. System Configuration
div.p: Since the concepts in this paper cross into the discipline of computer science, we present in this section a potential reference implementation for the ECS. We use sequence diagrams, like flowcharts, to express interactions between TDP/ECS system components using the Unified Modeling Language (UML), which the computer science field commonly uses to convey computer-related design concepts. Two diagrams are provided: one for system configuration (Figure 6) and another for the student-facing interface (Figure 7).

figure.head: ECS System Configuration
figure.figDesc: UML sequence diagram of the ECS configuration process, showing the Configurator actor setting criteria for each ECS face (Who, What, When, Where, How, Why) through the ECS Controller, then reviewing the resulting 5W1H Prompt Grid before ending the configuration.

div.p: Instructors, content managers, or researchers configure the questions and criteria for the six fundamental questions (5W1H) represented by the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS). (Refer to the two-dimensional Questions Grid in Figure 2 above for examples of criteria and constraints for each question.) In the ECS configuration sequence diagram, instructors or context managers are represented by the actor called Configurator. To manipulate the three-dimensional ECS, the Configurator interacts with the ECS Controller object and ECS Face entities.

The ECS Controller object is responsible for manipulating, maintaining, and storing the states of ECS Face entities. ECS Face entities are constructed as the Configurator rotates the ECS choosing either the binary sides or the faces of the nested Platonic solids. These ECS Face entities represent the components of the visual instantiation of the Event Cruncher Stylus:

list.item: Core Binary: The heart of the ECS is the fundamental binary distinction — typically actor/action (who/what) — that anchors the configuration logic.
Tetrahedron: Surrounding the core, the tetrahedron introduces spatiotemporal context (where/when), providing spatial and temporal scaffolding for event construction.
Cube: The next layer encodes causal relationships (how/why), adding mechanical and teleological reasoning to the spatiotemporal and binary actor/action contexts.

Octahedron: As the external interface and control device, the octahedron enables Configurator actors to input, edit, and validate the questions, criteria, and constraints for the contexts the ECS represents.

div.p: Configurator actors can also view the ECS configuration in two dimensions for validation. When the instructor/manager is satisfied that the configuration is adequate for use by students, the configuration process ends.

figure.head: Student-Facing Interface
figure.figDesc: UML sequence diagram of the Event Cruncher Stylus student-facing interface, showing message exchanges among the Student actor, ECS Controller, ECS Face, a large language model, Balance Validation, and the 5W1H Prompt Grid across the three TDP steps: 5W1H input and validation, AI generation, and scrutiny/review.

div.p: Learners add their sources, narrative, and media to the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS) for the six fundamental questions (5W1H) in Step 1 of the TDP process. The Student-Facing Interface diagram (Figure 7) maps out the full lifecycle of student engagement, from structured inquiry through critical reflection and — read alongside the three-step TDP method described in Section 4 — enacts that method in system-design terms: The population of ECS faces corresponds to Step 1, the dispatch of prompt and RAG data to the LLM and the generation of the simulation to Step 2, and the student’s review, annotation, and decision whether to iterate to Step 3. Like the process for configuration, the student actor iterates through each side and face of the ECS to input their data. Haptic feedback provides the student with forceful tactile separation between the six fundamental questions — Who?, What?, When?, Where?, Why?, How? — in this unique embodied way, consistent with the interpretive thick description advocated by anthropologist Clifford Geertz (1973). Note that haptic feedback can be simulated for devices that do not support true haptics. Lécuyer et al. (2009) have demonstrated that users can experience the illusion of mechanoreceptive sensory input using software that takes advantage of visual dominance in sensory conflict involving spatial properties. Simulating tactile feedback using visual cues, like slowing down the ratio between mouse movement and corresponding display response, is called pseudo-haptic feedback.

As the student actor inputs and validates their data, the ECS Controller may interface with an application programming interface (API) hosting a large language model (LLM) to perform contextual consistency checks. The ECS Controller builds a prompt for the large language model (LLM) from the data provided by the student actor. Sources provided by the student are added to the prompt as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) data, a technique in which specific documents or passages selected by the user are provided directly to the language model alongside the prompt, so that the model’s output draws on those specific sources rather than relying solely on patterns learned during training (lewis_etal 2020). This design choice has direct pedagogical consequences: By requiring students to supply their own sources as RAG data, TDP ensures that the simulation is constrained by the student’s research rather than only by the general statistical patterns of the model’s training corpus. The student’s simulation is built from the student’s sources in a configuration that counteracts the hallucination risk described in Section 2 and reinforces the poietic character of the method. The student’s research shapes what the AI can produce; the AI does not substitute for that research. Both the prompt and the RAG data are sent to the API hosting the large language model, and the LLM generates the narrative simulation. In Step 3 of the TDP process, the student actor reviews and evaluates the narrative simulation created by the generative AI, reflects on its alterity, and notes needed corrections. If changes are desired, the TDP process is repeated; otherwise, the TDP process is considered complete for the current iteration.

div.head: 8. Conclusion — True Digital Poiesis and the Future of Humanities Education
div.p: The emergence of generative AI challenges traditional models of humanities education by destabilizing long-held distinctions between authorship and simulation, research and reconfiguration, reality and representation. In this context, TDP offers a conceptual framework for navigating these challenges — not by resisting technological change, but by reimagining humanistic inquiry through it. At its core, TDP affirms that the poietic act of making, shaping, and interpreting remains central to the humanities, even in an age of algorithmic co-authorship. Far from automating historical understanding, generative tools become, within TDP, instruments of engagement: They render the learner not a passive consumer of synthetic media but an active constructor of historically aware simulations.

By embedding the hermeneutics of alterity by way of experiential learning into a structured, embodied, and reviewable process, TDP seeks to ensure that the use of AI in the classroom remains ethically grounded (by keeping the assumptions driving simulations as transparent as possible), intellectually rigorous, and pedagogically generative. The proposed tools are not merely technological enhancements; they are interfaces of reflection that bring into reach and view the assumptions and interpretive labor behind historical construction. The ECS, with its emphasis on tactility, balance, and physical manipulation, foregrounds composition as an embodied act. The critical review step teaches students to value historical thinking as a self-reflective iterative process of truing information: of bringing their representations of the past into the closest possible alignment with the evidence, while remaining aware that perfect alignment is neither achievable nor the goal.

TDP is offered here as a conceptual and design framework grounded in hermeneutic theory, experiential learning research, and Digital Humanities practice. The three-step method is being piloted in a prototype implementation at the University of Florida, and we have begun to gather observations about how students engage with the workflow. Systematic empirical evaluation of student outcomes — including assessment of historical thinking skills, critical engagement with AI-generated content, and understanding of alterity — remains to be conducted, and several key questions await further research: How does the TDP workflow perform across different historical periods, languages, and documentary traditions? Does the three-dimensional ECS interface produce measurably different learning outcomes from the flat Questions Grid? At what point in the iterative cycle do students develop genuine critical distance from the AI’s outputs, rather than accepting them as authoritative? And what happens when students discover that the LLM cannot be made to represent certain historical perspectives, regardless of the sources provided — how do instructors best use that discovery as a pedagogical moment? These are not gaps that disqualify the framework; they are the questions that a genuinely productive framework makes it possible — and necessary — to ask. That TDP generates them is itself evidence of its conceptual reach.

The 5W1H framework that structures TDP is also worth interrogating as a constraint as much as a resource. By structuring historical inquiry around these six questions, TDP necessarily foregrounds certain dimensions of historical experience — agency, causation, temporal and spatial location — while other dimensions may be less naturally captured: structures of feeling, sensory textures, the phenomenology of time lived rather than time measured, the experience of groups who left no records answerable to these questions. Future iterations of TDP should explore whether the framework can be extended or adapted to make these experiential residues more legible, or whether supplementary methods are required.

Looking ahead, the implications of TDP extend well beyond the study of the medieval and early modern world. As synthetic media proliferates across public discourse, the ability to analyze, contextualize, and responsibly re-make the past will become a crucial civic skill — one for which TDP offers a structured preparation, not merely in the academy but for the conditions of public life in a media environment shaped by generative AI. The practice of truing a simulation — submitting a confident-looking AI output to iterative scrutiny, revising the inputs, re-running the model, and recognizing that the result is still only a provisionally calibrated representation — generalizes beyond the history classroom as a discipline of critical engagement with AI-generated content that the current moment urgently requires. TDP provides a model for how the Humanities can thrive in the face of technological change: not by retreating into disciplinary isolation, but by asserting the importance of humanistic methods within digital environments, and by generating research questions that only the humanities is equipped to ask.

The Siege of Orléans: Voices of Faith and Fire
div.p: The Siege of Orléans: Voices of Faith and Fire

The year was 1429. For months, the French city of Orléans had suffered under the iron grip of English and Burgundian forces. Smoke rose from the outskirts, the air heavy with despair and the scent of burnt grain. Soldiers starved behind the city’s walls, praying for a miracle.

Across the fields of Domrémy, a young peasant girl named Joan of Arc claimed she had heard divine voices — saints urging her to save France. It is God’s will, she told the skeptical nobles. France shall rise again, and I shall lead her army to victory. Moved by her conviction, Charles VII granted her armor, a sword, and command of four thousand men. Dressed in silver plate and carrying a white banner adorned with Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and two angels, she rode toward Orléans.

Among the troops marching behind her were Jacques, a thin but sharp-eyed archer trained with a crossbow, and Louis, his closest friend, a swordsman. Do you truly believe she’s been sent by God? Louis asked as they crossed the Loire River.
Jacques adjusted his bowstring. I don’t know, he replied. But if her courage is heaven-sent, that’s enough for me.
When Joan entered Orléans on April 29, the city erupted in hope. Citizens leaned from windows, cheering. Soldiers who had nearly given up straightened their armor once more.
Fear not! Joan cried. The Lord is with us. We shall drive them out before the week’s end!

The following days brought fierce combat. The English garrisons, armed with longbows and cannons, rained fire upon the French positions. Joan rode through the smoke, rallying her men. Do not retreat! The victory is near! she shouted, lifting her banner high as arrows whistled past. Her voice, steady and sure, carried across the chaos.

At the Church of St. Loup, Jacques fired bolt after bolt into the enemy lines. Louis, sword in hand, charged through the breach beside Joan. For France! he cried, before being struck down in the melee. Joan knelt beside him briefly, whispering, You have served God well.

By May 7, the French launched a final assault on the bridge towers of Les Tourelles, the English stronghold over the Loire. Cannons thundered, fireboats set the river ablaze, and Joan, wounded by an arrow, still refused to fall back. In God’s name, we must press on! she commanded, her banner waving through the smoke.
By dawn, the English line broke. Trumpets sounded. The siege was over. On May 8, 1429, the battered French army stood victorious, and Orléans was free.
Jacques gazed at the sunrise over the Loire, the city safe once more. She’s just a girl, he murmured, but she’s changed everything.
News of the miracle spread across France. The victory at Orléans became a symbol of

divine favor and national pride, marking the turning point of the Hundred Years’ War. Joan of Arc’s faith had rekindled the spirit of a weary nation, and her name would forever stand among France’s greatest heroes and patron saints.
